problem.title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Anti-Entropy & Read-Repair Engine
problem.tagline: Combine R=2 digest-verified Read Repair for hot keys with background per-vnode Merkle tree sweeps over immutable SSTable snapshots, bounded by explicit gc_grace_seconds and I/O assumptions.
problem.purpose: When replicas in a leaderless key-value store miss writes during reboots or suffer silent disk corruption, you must decide how to heal both hot and cold keys without saturating cross-AZ links or resurrecting deleted data.

spark.summary: In a leaderless key-value store (exemplified by 100 nodes, RF=3, W=2, R=2), replicas diverge when node downtime exceeds hinted-handoff retention or when storage blocks corrupt silently. Pairing digest-based Read Repair on hot reads with background per-vnode Merkle tree sweeps converges both hot and cold ranges without full-replica scans.
spark.keyTakeaway: When multi-replica nodes reboot past hinted-handoff windows or risk silent disk corruption, pair lightweight digest checks on quorum reads with background Merkle tree sweeps over immutable storage snapshots, and enforce a deletion-retention quarantine policy so deleted keys cannot resurrect.
spark.byteSummary:
Foreground Read Repair only heals keys that clients actively query, leaving cold keys diverged after node outages. Full-replica scans across terabytes of data would saturate network and disk I/O.

Instead, quorum reads (`R=2`) fetch one full record and one 32-byte SHA-256 digest, triggering an asynchronous timestamp-ordered repair (`put_if_newer`) only when digests disagree. In the background, nodes build binary Merkle trees over immutable SSTable snapshots (with cached digests for unchanged cold SSTables) to isolate divergent token buckets in O(log L) steps.

Because deleted keys rely on tombstones that expire after `gc_grace_seconds`, nodes returning offline longer than the grace window cannot safely run standard anti-entropy without risking zombie-key resurrection and should be wiped and re-bootstrapped.

learningJourney.title: Why Cold Drift Persists & How Depth-15 Merkle Trees Bound Comparisons
learningJourney.purpose: State the explicit cluster assumptions, show the exact Merkle tree memory and bucket-size math, and distinguish tree comparison cost from data transfer.

explanation.foundation:
Suppose Node 14 in your 100-node key-value cluster reboots for 4 hours—one hour longer than your 3-hour hinted-handoff buffer. Writes still succeed at quorum ($W=2$ of $RF=3$), so nobody gets paged. Two weeks later, a peer disk fails and clients read stale profiles because **90% of cold keys were never touched by foreground Read Repair**.

**How a Merkle Tree Solves This Without Scanning Everything**: Imagine comparing 1 million customer records between Replica A and Replica B. Instead of streaming all 1 million records over the network, divide the sorted keys into buckets, compute a cryptographic fingerprint (SHA-256) for each bucket, and hash pairs of fingerprints upward into a binary tree. Replica A and Replica B compare the single 32-byte root hash first: if it matches, they are identical; if it differs, they descend **only** into mismatched branches and repair only the differing bucket.

**Illustrative Cluster Baseline**: Assume 100 nodes ($RF=3$, $W=2, R=2$) holding **500 TB raw** (5 TB/node; ~166.7 TB logical unique data ignoring compression and metadata). With 256 vnodes per node, the cluster manages 100 × 256 = 25,600 vnode ranges (~19.5 GB raw per vnode).
explanation.core:
**Merkle Tree Geometry & Memory Math**: Partition a vnode's token range into $L = 2^{15} = 32,768$ leaf buckets (depth $d = 15$). A complete binary tree with $L$ leaves has $2L - 1 = 65,535$ nodes. Storing one 32-byte SHA-256 hash per node takes:

$$65,535 \times 32\text{ B} \approx 2.1\text{ MB per vnode tree}$$

Keeping all 256 trees resident on one node uses 256 × 2.1 MB ≈ 537 MB RAM (or near-zero if built on demand per sub-range). Under **uniform key distribution**, each leaf averages $20\text{ GB} / 32,768 \approx 625\text{ KB}$. *Important*: 625 KB is an average under uniform keys, not a guaranteed repair size—hot partitions skew bucket sizes, and large outages still require streaming all diverged buckets.
explanation.deepDive: **Comparison vs. Repair Data**: A Merkle tree only guarantees $O(\log L)$ comparison steps to *locate* mismatched buckets (15 levels when 1 key differs). It does **not** bound total repaired bytes if thousands of buckets diverged after a long outage. As an illustrative floor, streaming at **50 MB/s** on a 5 TB node takes at least $5\times 10^6\text{ MB} / 50\text{ MB/s} \approx 27.8\text{ hours}$ of pure network transfer—assuming zero contention, no compaction overlap, and excluding tree-build disk I/O.

sectionDiagram.title: From 20 GB Vnode Scans to 625 KB Bucket Isolation (Uniform Assumption)
sectionDiagram.summary: Depth-15 trees (~2.1 MB/vnode) isolate single-bucket drift in 15 levels, while total repair time depends on divergence ratio and I/O limits.

learningJourney.title: Digest Read Repair: Quorum Mechanics, Deletes & Consistency Limits
learningJourney.purpose: Clarify what each replica returns on R=2 reads, how concurrent writes/tombstones are compared, and what consistency guarantees hold.

explanation.foundation: On a quorum read with $R = 2$ (out of $RF = 3$), the coordinator sends `get_full(key)` to the lowest-latency replica (Replica 1) and `get_digest(key)` to Replica 2. Replica 2 hashes `(value_or_tombstone, hlc)` and returns a **32-byte SHA-256 digest** instead of the full payload. If digests match, the coordinator returns Replica 1's value in 1 RTT.
explanation.core:
If digests differ, the coordinator fetches Replica 2's full record (including tombstones, which carry their own HLC), picks the winner via `(hlc_ms, hlc_seq, node_id)` (or Version Vectors), and fires an asynchronous `put_if_newer(key, winner)` to the stale replica.

**Consistency Boundary**: Under normal operation with strict quorums, $W + R = 2 + 2 = 4 > RF = 3$ ensures replica-set intersection. However, $W + R > RF$ alone **does not guarantee linearizability** under sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, or overlapping failures, and because `put_if_newer` runs asynchronously after returning to the client, Read Repair provides **eventual convergence**.

sectionDiagram.title: Digest Verification, Tombstone-Aware Merge & Async CAS Repair
sectionDiagram.summary: R=2 digest checks return immediately on match and heal stale replicas asynchronously using HLC compare-and-set.

steps.title: Parallel Full + Digest Read
steps.explanation: Coordinator fetches full value from Replica 1 and only a 32-byte digest from Replica 2.

steps.title: Detect Digest Mismatch
steps.explanation: Digests differ, so coordinator fetches Replica 2's full record and picks HLC=502 as winner.

steps.title: Async CAS Repair
steps.explanation: Client receives winning value immediately while Replica 2 is healed asynchronously with HLC CAS.

decisionFramework.problem: Two replicas return different versions of the same key during an R=2 quorum read.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Always fetch full payloads from all RF=3 replicas and block the client response until all replicas are repaired synchronously.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Doubles/triples internal read bandwidth on the 99.9% healthy path and couples client tail latency to the slowest replica.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Full-value quorum read + sync repair, vs. 32-byte digest check + asynchronous CAS repair.
decisionFramework.decision: Fetch 1 full value + 1 32-byte SHA-256 digest; fetch the second payload and trigger async put_if_newer only on mismatch.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Cuts healthy-path cross-node read bytes nearly in half, at the cost of repair completing asynchronously after the client ACK.

decisionExercise.prompt: During an R=2 quorum read, Replica 1 (HLC=502) and Replica 2 (HLC=490) return different digests, and Replica 3 is temporarily unreachable. What should the coordinator do?

options.text: Fail the read with 503 because Replica 3 is unreachable.
options.feedback: R=2 quorum is already satisfied by Replicas 1 and 2; failing availability violates quorum design.

options.text: Return HLC=502 to the client immediately and submit an async put_if_newer(502) to Replica 2 (and queue/hint for Replica 3).
options.feedback: Correct! Returning the newest quorum version keeps reads fast while async put_if_newer converges Replica 2.

options.text: Wait synchronously for Replica 3 to reboot before returning.
options.feedback: Blocking on an unreachable 3rd replica destroys read availability and p99 latency.

learningJourney.title: Capturing Stable Merkle Views Across MemTables, Flushes & Compaction
learningJourney.purpose: Explain how an LSM-tree storage engine freezes a consistent point-in-time view for Merkle tree building while writes and compaction continue.

explanation.foundation: Scanning live mutable structures over several minutes creates a **torn snapshot**: keys written mid-scan appear in some buckets and not others, causing identical replicas to compute different root hashes.
explanation.core:
To capture a stable view without blocking writes:
1. **Freeze active MemTable**: Rotate the mutable MemTable to an immutable MemTable (or record a monotonic sequence/LSN watermark) and reference the current list of immutable SSTable file descriptors (pinning them via reference counts so background compaction cannot unlink them mid-scan).
2. **Read via pinned view**: A merge-iterator reads the frozen MemTable + pinned SSTables for a **1.25 GB sub-range** (1/16th of a 20 GB vnode).
3. **Cache cold SSTable digests**: Because flushed L2–L4 SSTables are immutable, per-bucket digests for cold SSTables can be cached and folded only when new L0/L1 SSTables flush `(exact disk-I/O savings depend on your L0/L1 write amplification and compaction cadence)`.
explanation.deepDive: Pinning SSTable file descriptors briefly increases disk usage if compaction finishes replacing an SSTable while a sub-range scan is active; keeping sub-ranges small (~1.25 GB, finishing in seconds) bounds temporary disk retention.

sectionDiagram.title: Pinned MemTable + SSTable View While Compaction & Writes Continue
sectionDiagram.summary: Rotating the MemTable and reference-counting active SSTables gives Merkle builders a tear-free view without halting writes.

learningJourney.title: gc_grace_seconds Retention, Downtime Tracking & Zombie Prevention
learningJourney.purpose: Explain why tombstones expire, how downtime is tracked, and under what assumptions a quarantine-and-rebootstrap policy prevents zombie keys.

explanation.foundation: In an LSM-tree, `DELETE(K)` writes a **tombstone** `(key, TOMBSTONE, hlc)` rather than erasing `K` immediately—otherwise older SSTables or offline replicas would still hold `K`. Tombstones are retained for `gc_grace_seconds` (commonly configured to 10 days = 864,000s) before compaction purges them.
explanation.core:
**Zombie-Key Risk**: If Replica A deletes `K` at $t=0$ and purges its tombstone at $t=10\text{ days}$, while Replica B was offline for 12 days and still holds `K`, standard Merkle anti-entropy sees `K` on B and absent on A—and copies deleted `K` back onto A.

**Downtime Tracking & Quarantine Policy**: Track each node's `last_healthy_heartbeat_ts` (and per-vnode `last_repair_completed_ts`) in replicated cluster metadata (e.g., gossip + Raft/etcd membership). Under the policy assumption that all replicas must receive deletions within `gc_grace_seconds`, any node whose verified downtime exceeds `gc_grace_seconds` is **quarantined** from normal Merkle sync, wiped, and re-bootstrapped from a healthy peer's snapshot. *Limitation*: if a network partition prevents tracking true downtime or a tombstone was manually compacted early, a full cluster-wide read/sweep cannot distinguish purged deletes from missed writes.
explanation.deepDive: Pair this policy with I/O isolation: serialize active repair streams to 1 per physical NVMe drive and throttle repair bandwidth dynamically if foreground read latency crosses SLO.

sectionDiagram.title: Evaluating Downtime Against gc_grace_seconds Before Merkle Sync
sectionDiagram.summary: Quarantining nodes offline past gc_grace_seconds prevents purged deletions from resurrecting as zombie keys.

decisionExercise.prompt: Replica B has been offline for 12 days due to a rack power failure. Your cluster's tombstone retention (`gc_grace_seconds`) is 10 days, and healthy replicas have already compacted away deletions from days 1–2. Replica B comes back online. What should the cluster do?

options.text: Allow normal Merkle anti-entropy between Replica A and Replica B.
options.feedback: Unsafe! Replica A purged its tombstones at day 10, so Merkle sync would treat Replica B's old deleted keys as missing and resurrect them as zombies.

options.text: Quarantine Replica B from normal sync, wipe its stale SSTables, and re-bootstrap it from a healthy replica snapshot.
options.feedback: Correct! Under the gc_grace_seconds policy, re-bootstrapping from a healthy peer guarantees deleted keys stay deleted.

options.text: Delete all remaining tombstones on healthy replicas immediately.
options.feedback: Deleting tombstones early exposes even more old data to zombie resurrection.

learningJourney.title: Identifying Trustworthy Replicas & Isolating Corrupt SSTables
learningJourney.purpose: Explain how CRC32C block checksums and RF=3 quorum comparison distinguish silent bit-flips from legitimate stale data.

explanation.foundation: When two replicas disagree on a Merkle leaf hash, a hash mismatch alone does not tell you whether Replica B is merely **stale** (missed a write) or **corrupt** (suffered an NVMe bit-flip).
explanation.core:
1. **Local Integrity (CRC32C)**: Every 64 KB SSTable data block carries a CRC32C checksum. Any block failing CRC32C is immediately flagged corrupt and quarantined—never used as a repair source. *Note*: CRC32C detects storage bit-flips, **not** semantic bugs (e.g., if an application wrote bad data before the checksum was computed).
2. **Multi-Replica Disagreement**: When replicas pass CRC32C with differing hashes, comparing across $RF=3$ lets a **2-of-3 majority** isolate a single-node outlier. *Limitation*: a 2-of-3 match is not automatic proof of correctness against correlated bad writes or shared software bugs—it protects against independent single-replica corruption.

sectionDiagram.title: CRC32C Verification & 2-of-3 Majority Trust Selection
sectionDiagram.summary: Per-block CRC32C checks and 2-of-3 replica agreement isolate corrupt SSTables before they can poison healthy peers.

learningJourney.title: Assumptions, Limitations & Core Glossary
learningJourney.purpose: Document explicit architectural assumptions, failure boundaries, unverified workload estimates, and core distributed-KV terms.

explanation.foundation:
### Assumptions & Limitations
- **Replication & Quorum**: Assumes $RF = 3, W = 2, R = 2$ ($W + R > RF$) so reads intersect at least one up-to-date write replica under normal operation.
- **Clock Skew**: HLC LWW assumes bounded physical clock drift; extreme unmonitored clock skew can misorder concurrent independent writes unless Version Vectors or CRDTs are used.
- **Eventual Convergence**: Async Read Repair provides eventual convergence, not linearizability.
- **Workload-Dependent Estimates**: The ~27.8h transfer floor (5 TB / 50 MB/s) and cold-SSTable I/O savings depend on actual key skew, divergence ratio, and L0/L1 compaction cadence.
explanation.core:
### Concise Glossary
- **HLC (Hybrid Logical Clock)**: Combines physical wall time with a logical counter to preserve causal ordering despite small NTP clock skew.
- **RF (Replication Factor)**: Number of independent nodes storing a copy of each key range (e.g., $RF = 3$).
- **Quorum ($W, R$)**: Minimum replicas that must acknowledge a write ($W$) or respond to a read ($R$); $W + R > RF$ ensures overlap.
- **vnode (Virtual Node)**: A sub-range of the consistent-hash token ring assigned to a physical node to balance data and repair granularity.
- **SSTable (Sorted String Table)**: Immutable, sorted on-disk data file flushed from an LSM-tree MemTable.
- **Tombstone**: A deletion marker storing key + timestamp so deletes propagate before old values are purged.
- **Anti-Entropy**: Background replica comparison and synchronization (commonly via Merkle trees) that converges cold and hot data alike.
explanation.deepDive: When adapting this design to your own cluster, benchmark L0/L1 SSTable hash-build CPU and cross-AZ repair throughput under peak foreground read load before setting `gc_grace_seconds` and repair rate caps.

knowledgeChecks.question: During an `R=2` quorum read, why does the coordinator fetch a full payload from Replica 1 and only a 32-byte SHA-256 digest from Replica 2?

options.text: To cut cross-node read network bandwidth nearly in half when replicas agree, while still detecting mismatches for async Read Repair.
options.feedback: Correct! Only when digests differ does the coordinator fetch Replica 2's full payload and trigger Read Repair.

options.text: Because Replica 2 only stores hashes and never stores actual values.
options.feedback: All RF=3 replicas store full values; digest reads are a bandwidth optimization.

options.text: Because SHA-256 digests can be reversed to reconstruct the original JSON payload.
options.feedback: SHA-256 is one-way; Replica 2's full value is fetched only on mismatch.

options.text: To bypass HLC timestamp ordering.
options.feedback: HLC timestamps are used whenever a mismatch is detected.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Digest reads verify quorum agreement with 32 bytes instead of streaming duplicate full payloads on every read.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is background Merkle anti-entropy still mandatory even when foreground Read Repair is enabled on 100% of reads?

options.text: Read Repair only heals keys that clients actively read; cold keys and un-read silent bit-flips would remain diverged forever.
options.feedback: Correct! Cold tail data (often 90%+ of a 500 TB store) relies on background Merkle sweeps to stay converged.

options.text: Read Repair only works on single-node deployments.
options.feedback: Read Repair is specifically a multi-replica quorum mechanism.

options.text: Read Repair deletes tombstones before gc_grace_seconds expires.
options.feedback: Compaction purges tombstones, not Read Repair.

options.text: Read Repair cannot use HLC timestamps.
options.feedback: Read Repair uses the exact same HLC/Version-Vector merge rules.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Foreground Read Repair cannot heal cold keys that are rarely or never read by clients.

knowledgeChecks.question: How does caching leaf-bucket digests per immutable cold L2-L4 SSTable improve background anti-entropy at 500 TB scale?

options.text: It eliminates re-hashing unchanged cold SSTables on every repair cycle, cutting background disk read I/O by ~80%.
options.feedback: Correct! Only newly flushed L0/L1 SSTables need fresh hashing before folding into the vnode Merkle tree.

options.text: It removes the need for consistent hashing vnodes.
options.feedback: Vnodes still partition the token ring; SSTable caching speeds up tree construction within each vnode.

options.text: It allows nodes offline for 60 days to skip gc_grace_seconds checks.
options.feedback: Stale-node quarantine past gc_grace_seconds is still strictly required.

options.text: It doubles the replication factor from RF=3 to RF=6.
options.feedback: Replication factor is unchanged.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Immutable SSTables never change once written, so their bucket digests can be cached and reused across repair cycles.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does building a Merkle tree over a live, mutating MemTable without freezing/pinning snapshots cause false repair storms?

options.text: Keys written mid-scan appear in some buckets and not others (a torn snapshot), causing identical idle replicas to produce different root hashes.
options.feedback: Correct! Rotating the MemTable and reference-counting active SSTables gives the tree builder a tear-free point-in-time view.

options.text: MemTables cannot store SHA-256 hashes.
options.feedback: Hashes are computed by the tree builder; the issue is concurrent mutation during the scan.

options.text: Pinning SSTables disables CRC32C checksums.
options.feedback: CRC32C remains active on every block read.

options.text: Freezing the MemTable deletes un-flushed writes.
options.feedback: Frozen MemTables remain readable and flush normally to L0 SSTables.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: A tear-free snapshot (frozen MemTable + pinned SSTable descriptors) ensures replicas compute consistent Merkle trees while writes continue.

knowledgeChecks.question: A 64 KB SSTable block passes its CRC32C checksum on Replica 1 and Replica 2, yet their values differ for the same key. What does passing CRC32C prove?

options.text: Only that the bytes on disk match what was checksummed when written—not semantic correctness or which version is causally newer.
options.feedback: Correct! CRC32C catches storage bit-flips, whereas HLC/Version Vectors and quorum comparison resolve version divergence.

options.text: That Replica 1's value is guaranteed to be globally linearizable.
options.feedback: CRC32C is a local block-integrity check, not a distributed consistency proof.

options.text: That the key has no deletion tombstones.
options.feedback: Tombstones are also checksummed inside SSTable blocks.

options.text: That Replica 3 is offline.
options.feedback: CRC32C is purely local to each SSTable block.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: CRC32C verifies storage-level bit integrity, not distributed version ordering or semantic correctness.

knowledgeChecks.question: Does a depth-15 Merkle tree (`32,768` leaves) guarantee that anti-entropy repair will transfer at most `625 KB` of data?

options.text: No—625 KB is only an average leaf size under uniform keys when 1 bucket differs; skewed keys or many diverged buckets require streaming all affected buckets.
options.feedback: Correct! Merkle trees bound comparison steps to O(log L) to locate drift, not total bytes repaired.

options.text: Yes—SHA-256 compresses every bucket to 625 KB.
options.feedback: SHA-256 produces a 32-byte hash for comparison; actual key-value records must still be streamed on mismatch.

options.text: Yes—unless gc_grace_seconds is disabled.
options.feedback: Repair byte volume depends on divergence ratio and key distribution.

options.text: No—because Merkle trees always stream the entire 20 GB vnode.
options.feedback: Matching subtrees are pruned, so only mismatched buckets are streamed.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Merkle trees bound comparison cost to O(log L), while actual repair transfer scales with the number and size of mismatched buckets.

beginner.keyTakeaway: When multi-replica nodes reboot past hinted-handoff windows or suffer silent disk corruption, pair lightweight 32-byte checksum reads on hot keys with background Merkle hash-tree sweeps for cold ranges, and wipe any node offline longer than your deletion retention window so deleted keys never come back to life.
beginner.byteSummary: Even with 3 copies of every record, one server can miss an update during a reboot. Checking a quick fingerprint on reads fixes popular keys right away, while Merkle trees sweep the rest of the database efficiently.

intermediate.byteSummary:
In a 100-node leaderless key-value store (replication factor `N=3`, quorum `W=2, R=2`, 500 TB total data), replicas continuously drift when nodes reboot past hinted-handoff windows, network partitions drop async writes, or silent NVMe bit-flips corrupt SSTables. Relying solely on foreground **Read Repair** only heals hot keys that clients happen to read—leaving cold 99% tail data silently rotting.

A production **Anti-Entropy & Read-Repair Engine** pairs foreground digest-based Read Repair (fetching 1 full value + `R-1` lightweight SHA-256 digests on `R=2` reads) with background **Per-Vnode Merkle Tree Anti-Entropy**. Each node partitions its 256 vnodes into depth-15 Merkle trees built over immutable SSTable snapshots, exchanges root and mismatched subtree hashes over gRPC, and streams only divergent leaf buckets using Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) LWW or Version Vector merges.

Crucially, the engine enforces an I/O-throttled compaction-aware repair scheduler, hashes deletion tombstones within a 10-day `gc_grace_seconds` window, and quarantines nodes offline past `gc_grace_seconds` for clean snapshot re-bootstrap so zombie keys never resurrect.

prerequisites.title: 1. Replication Factor (RF) & Virtual Nodes
prerequisites.summary: To survive disk or server crashes, each key is copied onto RF=3 different servers. Each server's hash range is split into smaller virtual nodes (vnodes) so data and repairs spread evenly.

prerequisites.title: 2. Quorum Reads & Writes (W + R > RF)
prerequisites.summary: If a write waits for W=2 servers and a read checks R=2 servers (out of 3), at least one server overlaps under normal operation—though asynchronous repair or sloppy quorums can still leave stale copies.

prerequisites.title: 3. Hinted Handoff
prerequisites.summary: When a replica is briefly down, peers temporarily hold 'hints' of missed writes for a few hours. Once a node stays offline past that window, hints are dropped and background repair is needed.

prerequisites.title: 4. What a Merkle Tree Is (and Why It Exists)
prerequisites.summary: Instead of streaming 1 million records between Replica A and Replica B to find 1 mismatch, group keys into buckets, hash each bucket with SHA-256, and pair hashes into a tree. If two subtree hashes match, skip that entire half.

_nextProblem.prompt: Design a multi-terabyte Data Engineering platform that ingests clickstream and order CDC events from Kafka at 100,000 events/sec, deduplicates and enriches them in near real-time (< 2 min freshness), and serves BI + ML feature consumers via a Medallion Lakehouse.
